title: Circuit breaker

definition.text: A design pattern that wraps calls to a remote service, watches for failures and stops making the calls once failures pass a threshold, so failures do not cascade.

facts.text: The protected call is wrapped in a circuit breaker object that monitors for failures; once failures reach a threshold the breaker trips and all further calls return an error without the protected call being made.
Remote calls, unlike in-memory calls, can fail or hang until a timeout; many callers on an unresponsive supplier can exhaust critical resources and cause cascading failures across systems.
Unlike timeout-only methods, which delay error responses or fail healthy requests prematurely, a circuit breaker detects unresponsive services dynamically and prevents repeated attempts.
Breakers monitor service health through heartbeats, synthetic transactions or real-time usage monitoring.
The pattern is used together with retry, fallback and timeout patterns to strengthen fault tolerance.
Marc Brooker warns that circuit breakers can read a partial failure as total failure and bring down the whole system; sharded and cell-based systems are especially vulnerable.
A workaround is for the server to say which part is overloaded so the client uses a matching mini circuit breaker, but this is complex and expensive.
In cell-based microservices, breakers inside a cell limit cascading failures between services, while inter-cell breakers isolate failing cells and redirect traffic to cells that still work.

title: Circuit breaker states
article: Circuit breaker design pattern#Different states of circuit breaker

definition.text: A circuit breaker is in one of three states, closed, open or half-open, which decide whether calls reach the protected service.

facts.text: When everything is normal the breaker stays closed and all requests pass through; if failures rise beyond the threshold, the breaker trips into the open state.
In the open state the breaker returns an error immediately without invoking the service, and it moves to half-open after a timeout period that a monitoring system usually specifies.
In the half-open state a limited number of requests pass through; if they succeed the breaker returns to closed, and if they keep failing it goes back to open.
A monitor alert is usually wanted whenever the breaker trips.

definition.text: Retry strategies set how long a client waits between attempts after a transient error, so network instability is handled without overloading the service.

facts.text: Linear backoff waits a progressively increasing fixed interval between attempts; it is simple, but under high load or high concurrency it can cause resource contention or retry storms.
Linear jitter backoff adds a random jitter to each linearly growing interval, spreading retries over time, though synchronized retries remain possible because the base interval grows only linearly.

Exponential backoff increases the delay exponentially, for example 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds up to a maximum; it cuts load and suits high-load systems but can delay a fix that a quick retry would have achieved.

Exponential jitter backoff applies additive or multiplicative randomness after each exponential increase, reducing retry collisions further, though large jitter can cause longer delays than necessary.

definition.text: An operation is executed exactly once when it runs at least once and at most once at the same time.

facts.text: A payment system must execute each payment order exactly once, because double charging a customer is one of the most serious problems a payment system can have.
Exactly-once delivery looks hard, but it becomes easier when split in two: at-least-once is implemented with retry and at-most-once with an idempotency check.
Retry provides the at-least-once guarantee: a client retries a payment after a network error or timeout, and it may only succeed at a later attempt.
An idempotency key, usually a client-generated UUID that expires after a period, is sent in an HTTP header such as idempotency-key so the server can discard duplicate payment requests.

Exactly-once processing is generally not achievable across a network, but at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent processing gives the same observable result, called effectively-once processing.

title: Idempotency

definition.text: An operation is idempotent if applying it several times has the same effect as applying it once.

facts.text: Setting a user's email to a@example.com is idempotent, while 'add $10 to the balance' is not, because every repeat changes the result; a subroutine with side effects is idempotent if repeated calls leave the same system state as one call.
Networks drop responses, clients time out and load balancers retry, so the same request often reaches a server more than once.

After a payment request times out, the client cannot tell if the server missed it, processed it with a lost response, or is still processing; retrying without idempotency can charge the customer twice.

Idempotency lets an operation be retried as often as necessary without unintended effects, so reliable systems can run on unreliable networks and clients can retry aggressively; non-idempotent operations force the server to track whether they already ran.
Message brokers mostly offer at-least-once delivery so consumers see duplicates, and idempotency also guards against duplicate submissions from double-clicks or page refreshes.
Looking up a customer, changing an address and canceling an order are idempotent, but placing an order is not, since multiple requests place multiple orders.

HTTP standards say GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent and POST need not be; idempotent means the same server state after one or many calls, not an identical response, so a repeated DELETE may return 404.
Idempotency is not free: it needs extra storage and lookups for keys and extra logic for concurrent and in-flight requests.

notes: Wikipedia's Idempotence page is the article; its abstract-algebra and function examples are left out as mathematics. Extended with chunk 3 sentences.

definition.text: Idempotency is essential wherever an operation might be retried or executed multiple times.

facts.text: For RESTful API requests, retrying must not execute the same operation multiple times, so idempotent methods such as PUT and DELETE keep resource states consistent.

In payment processing, retries and network issues must not charge a customer several times, and in order management, submitting an order several times must place one order and not deduct inventory twice.
In user account management, a retried registration must not create multiple accounts, and several password reset requests must result in a single reset.

Reapplying a database transaction must not change the state beyond the first application, and reprocessing queue messages must not duplicate processing, so handlers must tolerate repeated messages without side effects.

definition.text: An idempotency key is a unique value, usually a UUID, that a client sends with a request that is not naturally idempotent so the server can detect duplicates.

facts.text: For operations that are not naturally idempotent, such as POST /payments, the client generates a unique key and sends it with the request, for example in an Idempotency-Key header.
The server looks up the key; if absent it stores the key, processes the request and saves the response against the key; if present it skips processing and returns the saved response.
Checking for the key and recording it must be atomic, or two concurrent retries can both pass the check; a database unique constraint or a Redis SET NX can do this.
The server should store a hash of the request payload and reject a repeated key that arrives with a different payload rather than return an unrelated saved response.
A retry can arrive while the original is still processing; the server can return a 409 Conflict or make the retry wait.
Keys do not need to live forever: a retention period of a few hours to a few days is common and keeps storage cost bounded.
Many tech companies, such as Stripe and PayPal, recommend a UUID as the idempotency key, sent in an HTTP header on payment requests.

definition.text: An idempotent consumer handles a message that arrives more than once so that the repeat has no extra effect.

facts.text: Message brokers usually guarantee at-least-once delivery, so a consumer must handle duplicates.
A deduplication table stores the ID of each processed message and skips a message whose ID is already present; the ID should be written in the same transaction as the side effect.
Natural idempotency designs the operation so repeating it is harmless, for example 'set status to shipped' instead of 'advance status'.
Versioning attaches a version or sequence number to updates and ignores any update that is not newer than the current state.

title: Rate limiting

definition.text: Rate limiting prevents the frequency of an operation from exceeding a defined limit.

facts.text: Large-scale systems use rate limiting to protect underlying services and resources; it is a defensive mechanism that lets shared resources stay available.
It protects APIs from unintended or malicious overuse by limiting how many requests can reach the API in a given period.
It avoids resource starvation caused by denial-of-service attacks, limits web scraping and can mitigate some other common attacks.
It controls operational costs by putting a virtual cap on auto-scaling, which unmonitored could lead to exponential bills.
It also controls data flow for APIs that process massive amounts of data, and data centers use it to share resources among tenants and applications according to their service level agreement.

A server checks the user session or IP address against a session cache, often a central in-memory key-value store such as Redis or Aerospike, and HTTP servers can answer too many requests with status 429.
Over the limit, a server or device offloads new requests without responding or queues them, but at peak times the request rate can exceed the queue capacity and requests are thrown away.
A hardware appliance limiting by IP address on layer 4 risks blocking a whole network of users behind one NAT address, so for dynamic content the limiting logic should be built into the application.

notes: Extended with chunk 3 (Wikipedia Rate limiting) sentences.

definition.text: The main rate-limiting algorithms are leaky bucket, token bucket, fixed window, sliding log and sliding window, each with its own advantages and disadvantages.

facts.text: Leaky bucket appends each request to a queue that is processed first-in, first-out at a regular interval; when the queue is full, additional requests are discarded.
Token bucket requires each request to take a token from a bucket; with no token available the request is refused and the requester must try again later, and the bucket refreshes after a time period.
Fixed window tracks a counter for a window of n seconds, increments it on each request and discards the request when the counter exceeds a threshold.
Sliding log keeps a time-stamped log for each request in a time-sorted hash set or table and discards logs whose timestamps are beyond a threshold.
For a new request, sliding log sums the logs to find the request rate and holds the request if it would exceed the threshold rate.
Sliding window is a hybrid that keeps fixed window's low processing cost and sliding log's better boundary behavior, adding a weighted value of the previous window's rate to smooth traffic bursts.

definition.text: Rate limiting across a cluster of nodes is hard because of inconsistent per-node counters and race conditions on shared counters.

facts.text: A cluster may need a global rate limit; if each node tracks its own, a consumer can exceed the global limit by sending requests to different nodes, and more nodes make that likelier.
Sticky sessions in the load balancer send each consumer to exactly one node, but cause a lack of fault tolerance and scaling problems.
A centralized data store such as Redis is another approach, but it increases latency and causes race conditions.
A naive get-then-set counter reads, increments and writes back; extra requests slip in during that cycle and store stale lower values, letting a consumer bypass the limit.
A distributed lock around the counter key prevents that race, but the lock becomes a significant bottleneck and does not scale well.
A set-then-get approach lets counters be incremented and checked quickly without atomic operations getting in the way.

title: Resilience patterns

definition.text: Resilience patterns are cloud design patterns that reduce the damage failures do, so a small error does not snowball into an outage.

facts.text: The largest incidents are usually caused by something very small: a minor error starts a snowball effect and suddenly everything is down.
Patterns that reduce the damage of failures include circuit breaker, rate limiting, load shedding, back pressure and let it crash.
These patterns are usually not used alone; applying them well means understanding why each is needed, how it works and its limitations.

title: Exponential backoff

definition.text: Exponential backoff is an algorithm that uses feedback to multiplicatively decrease the rate of a process, to gradually find an acceptable rate.

facts.text: It is a closed-loop control that reduces the rate of a process in response to adverse events such as a collision, packet loss, an error response from a service or an explicit request to back off.
If a mobile app fails to connect it retries 1 second later, then 2 seconds, then 4 seconds; each time the pause is multiplied by a fixed amount, here 2.
The delay is an exponential function of the number of adverse events observed, with a multiplicative base; a base of 2 is called binary exponential backoff.
In rate limiting, each time a service says a client sends too often, the client cuts its rate by a predetermined factor until it reaches an acceptable equilibrium.

Unlike a fixed rate limit, backoff limits rates dynamically without giving the client prior information, and under heavy load or disruption it automatically lowers request rates, keeping some availability instead of overloading the service.

TCP retransmits a segment when its timer expires with a new timeout of twice the previous value, and WebSocket clients SHOULD delay reconnect attempts by increasingly longer amounts, for example with truncated binary exponential backoff.
Message-queue clients that are told to back off can retry the request later, perhaps with an exponential backoff strategy.

notes: History and theory section (ALOHA, Lam's adaptive backoff, expected backoff maths) not drafted: network-research history, not interview material.

definition.text: Truncated exponential backoff caps the number of increases so that the delay stops growing after a limit.

facts.text: The truncated variant limits the number of adverse events counted, so after a certain number of increases the exponentiation stops; without a limit the delay can become undesirably long.
Limiting the count reduces unexpectedly long latencies and improves recovery times after a transient outage.
In IEEE 802.3 CSMA/CD the ceiling is 10, so the maximum delay is 1023 slot times.
Choosing the limit balances collision probability against latency: a higher ceiling cuts collisions exponentially but widens the range of possible latencies and raises the average latency.

definition.text: Jitter adds randomness to backoff delays so that many senders or clients that fail together do not retry at the same moment.

facts.text: A deterministic backoff is unsuitable for shared channels because every sender would back off the same time, retransmit together and collide again.

So the time between retransmissions is randomized, and the exponential algorithm sets the range of possible delays: 0 or 1 slot times after the first collision, 0 to 3 after the second, 0 to 7 after the third.
A wider range of delays lowers the probability of a collision but increases the average latency.

In retry strategies, jitter can be additive, adding a random amount to the exponential delay, or multiplicative, multiplying it by a random factor; it reduces retry collisions but a large jitter can cause longer delays than necessary.

definition.text: Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to contain the propagation of faults and keep operating without failure while some components are faulty.

facts.text: Faults may show up as errors, such as a bad data value or missing message, that cause incorrect system state; fault-tolerant systems mask the errors and maintain failure-free operation despite one or more faulty components.
The capability is essential for high-availability, mission-critical and life-critical systems.
Strictly, it means handling faults with no degradation or downtime and users unaware of any issue; a system that suffers some interruption or graceful degradation of performance is termed resilient.

It requires no single point of failure, fault isolation to the failing component through dedicated failure detection, fault containment so a failure does not propagate, and reversion modes that abandon recent changes.
Fault-tolerant systems are typically based on redundancy and are judged by availability expressed as a percentage; a five nines system statistically provides 99.999% availability.

Making every component fault tolerant is normally not an option because redundancy costs weight, size, power, money and design time, so choose by how critical, how likely to fail and how expensive each component is.
A system that rarely has problems is not necessarily fault tolerant: one that fails only rarely but stops operating completely when a fault occurs is fault resistant, not fault tolerant.

title: Fault tolerance techniques

definition.text: Fault tolerance techniques use spare or independent components, such as replicas, standbys, load balancing and monitoring, so that a failure does not stop the service.

facts.text: Replication runs multiple identical instances in parallel, sends requests to all of them and picks the correct result by quorum; ByteByteGo describes it more broadly as multiple copies of data or services across nodes or locations.
Redundancy provides multiple identical instances and switches to a remaining one when a failure occurs, which is failover; redundancy means additional components that can take over.
Diversity provides multiple different implementations of the same specification and uses them like replicas, to cope with errors in one specific implementation.
Load balancing distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers so no single server becomes a point of failure, and failover mechanisms automatically switch to a standby when the primary fails.

Continuous monitoring of system health and performance, with alerts for anomalies or failures, completes the six principles ByteByteGo lists: replication, redundancy, load balancing, failover, graceful degradation, monitoring.
Every RAID level except RAID 0 is a fault-tolerant storage device that uses data redundancy.
The circuit breaker design pattern is a technique to avoid catastrophic failures in distributed systems.

notes: Hardware voting schemes in the Replication section (DMR, TMR, lockstep, pair-and-spare) left out as hardware-level detail.

definition.text: A system with graceful degradation keeps running at reduced functionality or performance after a component fails instead of failing completely.

facts.text: A system designed for graceful degradation, or to fail soft, operates at a reduced level of performance after some component fails rather than stopping.
Examples are a building that runs lighting at reduced levels after a grid failure, and a video stream that falls back to a lower-resolution version when network bandwidth is insufficient.
Progressive enhancement is another example: web pages are available in a basic functional format for limited browsers and in an enhanced version for capable ones.
In resilience, the system adapts to the error and maintains service while accepting some impact on performance.

definition.text: A fail-fast component reports at the first point of failure, and a fail-safe design fails in a way that protects people, property or data.

facts.text: A fail-fast component is designed to report at the first point of failure rather than after downstream components fail, which allows easier diagnosis and may prevent improper operation in a broken state.
A system designed to fail safe does so in a way that protects people, property or data from injury, damage, intrusion or disclosure, whether it keeps working at a reduced level or fails completely.
A program can fail safe by exiting gracefully instead of crashing in an uncontrolled way, to prevent data corruption after an error.
Singh's guide advises microservices to fail fast by using a circuit breaker to achieve fault tolerance.

title: Leaky bucket

definition.text: The leaky bucket is an algorithm based on the analogy of a bucket with a constant leak that overflows if water is poured in faster than it leaks or all at once beyond its capacity.

facts.text: It checks whether a sequence of discrete events conforms to limits on average and peak rates, and can limit the actions tied to those events to those rates or delay them until they conform.

As a meter, a counter is incremented as each packet or event arrives and decremented at a fixed rate; the event conforms if the counter stays below a limit value, meaning the bucket does not overflow.
In the original description, the decrement rate sets the average bandwidth and the threshold sets burstiness, and the network discards a packet if the counter exceeds the threshold when incremented.
As a queue, it is a finite FIFO buffer serviced at a fixed rate: an arrival is appended if there is room and discarded otherwise, and one packet is sent per clock tick.
For API rate limiting, the queue version appends each request to the end of a queue, processes the first item at a regular interval, and discards or leaks additional requests when the queue is full.
The queue implementation is always a traffic shaping function that sends at a fixed rate, though the output has gaps if the queue becomes empty.
The queue version is a special case of the meter version.
It is used in packet-switched and telecommunications networks for traffic policing, traffic shaping and scheduling of data transmissions to defined limits on bandwidth and burstiness.

notes: Wikipedia's ATM generic cell rate algorithm detail, emission interval, delay variation tolerance and maximum burst size sections left out as telecom parameter detail.

definition.text: Traffic policing drops or downgrades traffic that exceeds a limit, while traffic shaping delays it until it conforms.

facts.text: In traffic policing, packets that do not conform to the limits may be dropped or reduced in priority, for downstream traffic management to drop if there is congestion.
In traffic shaping, packets are delayed until they conform to the limits.
Both are commonly used to protect the network against excess or excessively bursty traffic.
Hosts commonly shape traffic at their network interfaces so that their transmissions are not discarded by traffic management functions in the network.

title: Token bucket

definition.text: The token bucket is an algorithm that checks whether traffic conforms to limits on bandwidth and burstiness, using a bucket that fills with tokens at a fixed rate.

facts.text: A fixed-capacity bucket gets a token every 1/r seconds and holds at most b tokens; a token arriving at a full bucket is discarded.
A packet of n bytes conforms if at least n tokens are in the bucket, which removes n tokens and sends the packet; otherwise no tokens are removed and the packet is non-conformant.
In API rate limiting, each request must take a token, and a request is refused when no token is available, so the requester has to try again later as the bucket refreshes.
Non-conformant packets can be queued until enough tokens accumulate, or sent marked as non-conformant and possibly dropped later if the network is overloaded.
A conforming flow can have an average rate up to the token rate and a burstiness set by the depth of the bucket; over the long run the conformant output is limited by the token rate r.
It can be used for traffic shaping, where packets are delayed until they conform, or for traffic policing, where nonconforming packets are dropped or reduced in priority.
It also controls database IO flow, where the limit applies to a linear combination of IOPS and bandwidth rather than to either alone.

notes: Burst-size formulas (Tmax, Bmax) not drafted: the dossier sentences carry formulas that lost their notation.

definition.text: The hierarchical token bucket is an arrangement of token buckets in a hierarchy that limits each client's rate so that no client saturates the total bandwidth.

facts.text: It is a faster replacement for the class-based queueing discipline in Linux, useful for limiting each client's download or upload rate so a limited client cannot saturate the total bandwidth.
Conceptually it is an arbitrary number of token buckets arranged in a hierarchy, with each class given a rate, its guaranteed bandwidth, and a ceil, the maximum bandwidth it may consume.
A class that requests more than its guaranteed bandwidth may borrow from its parent as long as both ceils are not reached.
Traffic shaping only helps at the bottleneck between the LAN and the Internet, typically a home or office LAN served by a DSL or T1 connection.

definition.text: The token bucket and the leaky bucket as a meter are mirror images that classify exactly the same traffic as conforming, while the leaky bucket as a queue is a different, shaping-only variant.

facts.text: The token bucket is directly comparable to the leaky bucket as a meter, its mirror image: conforming packets add fluid to a finite bucket that drains at a constant rate, matching tokens removed and added at a fixed rate.
Fundamentally the two algorithms are the same: implemented correctly with the same parameters they see exactly the same packets as conforming and nonconforming.
The leaky bucket as a queue is a special case of the meter version, applies only to traffic shaping and gives jitter-free output, so it differs significantly from the token bucket.
Both versions are described in the literature under the same name, which has caused considerable confusion over the leaky bucket's properties.
